codex.worst_flaw: The planned comparison uses the three weeks when both groups are eligible for the reward, so it cannot estimate what the reward adds to the shared workflow and feedback.

claude.worst_flaw: The weekly audit samples only 20 credited jobs, checks just timing and responses against job records, and has no independent observation of whether the checks were actually done. That leaves pencil-whipped checklists that tick every box largely undetected, while the main success metric (company-wide pre-start digital completion) can be inflated by delayed job-start entries.

holistic.reason: Well-designed with union co-design, workflow fixes, fairness rules, audit sampling and a stepped-wedge evaluation, but one paid hour is a modest reward that may go unnoticed, and the checklist-first screen change is the only thing carrying adoption after the incentive ends.

codex.worst_flaw: The specified three-week overlap cannot isolate the reward’s effect because both groups are earning rewards during that period.

claude.worst_flaw: The 60%-of-eligible-jobs threshold is not set from each technician's baseline or feasibility, and a technician with very few eligible jobs is not handled; a single pass/fail payout also gives anyone already above 60% no reason to improve, or to stay careful on the remaining jobs.

holistic.reason: Strong union co-design, paid time, offline support, privacy, anti-pressure audits and a staggered control make it approvable, but the setup is complex, the reward is modest, and durable habit hinges on the workflow fixes rather than two hours of time off.

claude.worst_flaw: The crew-level 80% threshold is set without any baseline or feasibility check and is never adjusted for crew size or case mix. The staggered comparison also has no predefined sample size, cost or harm outcomes, or uncertainty handling, and it has no independent shadow validation of the timestamp-ordering data before pay depends on it.

codex.worst_flaw: The pilot is unsafe to launch because crews can earn credit for marking hazards clear without an independent check that technicians actually assessed those hazards before starting work.

holistic.reason: Union-agreed, fair, well-guarded design with quality sampling, offline handling and a staggered rollout, but a 30-minute early finish is a modest reward and durability after it ends rests on the app fixes and habit rather than ongoing incentive.

claude.worst_flaw: The learning design is a phased before-and-after comparison on one team, with no comparison group, uncertainty handling or predefined harm and cost measures (such as review defect escape, author wait after the first review, or evening work), so the effect of the reward cannot be separated from the workflow fixes or ordinary drift.

codex.worst_flaw: The single-team pilot cannot distinguish the reward’s effect from improvements as engineers settle into the new review workflow.

holistic.reason: It fixes the actual bottleneck first (rotation, protected time, oldest-first queue), uses private feedback and a team-wide reward with no rankings, and has clear quality checks and an exit plan, but two hours of paid time off is a modest incentive, the weekly sampling and the manual disputes add overhead, and it is a lot of machinery for a sceptical 25-person team.

codex.worst_flaw: A rubber-stamp approval can pass the audit by naming a check, because the audit never verifies whether the review caught substantive issues.

claude.worst_flaw: A group-wide half-day off tied to an 80% on-time threshold creates all-or-nothing peer pressure and a free-rider risk, and nothing tests whether it adds value beyond the workflow fixes except a confounded two-week stagger, so it can't be justified as worth adding for sceptical engineers.

holistic.reason: The design is careful and sceptic-friendly (fix the workflow first, a time-off reward, private feedback, quality sampling, a no-individual-ranking rule), but it is complex to run, the 80% bar may be hard to hit, and lasting change depends on whether the workflow defaults stay in place once the reward ends.

claude.worst_flaw: The group reward is all or nothing at 85%, yet the design never deals with authors who can delay marking a PR ready to protect the measure, never says how disputed credit is appealed or how the event history can be replayed, and never checks review quality or cooperation after the reward ends.

codex.worst_flaw: The pilot sets no decision rule for whether the paid half-day improves response times enough beyond the queue fixes and private feedback to justify its cost and any loss of review quality or sprint capacity.

holistic.reason: It fixes the real queue friction first, uses a team-level half-day reward, tight anti-gaming rules and a pre-agreed exit decision, which suits sceptical engineers, though the elaborate rules and a four-week reward window may leave some engineers cold and limit how much the habit survives once the reward ends.

codex.worst_flaw: The reward lacks a representative field validation gate to establish that anonymous kiosk entries can be matched reliably to observed hand-hygiene moments across wards and shifts.

claude.worst_flaw: The main thing being measured is anonymous matching of kiosk entries to observer-sampled moments. This is untested and may not be possible, and there is no replayable event history or staffed appeal path to back it up. It also rewards documentation coverage, a logging proxy, when the clinical goal is hand hygiene itself.

holistic.reason: Well-guarded, staggered and safety-aware with an audit-validated reward, but the matching logistics are complex, the team meal is a weak, delayed motivator, and little structurally sustains logging once the prize ends.

codex.worst_flaw: The pilot cannot reliably establish whether nurses log eligible hand-hygiene moments because extra kiosk entries can offset missed entries within the same audit window.

claude.worst_flaw: The reward depends on sparse monthly observer audits, and the design never deals with the Hawthorne effect or with how few observations each ward gets, so a pooled audit over two periods can pass or fail a ward through noise, and nothing beyond the existing protocol sets a minimum sample or confidence check.

holistic.reason: Well-designed with payout tied to independent audits, anti-gaming safeguards and a staggered pilot, but the audit-based, monthly-lagged ward reward is a weak immediate motivator and some nurses may barely notice it beyond the kiosk.

claude.worst_flaw: The design never says why kiosk logging is worth doing: it rewards logging coverage without showing that logging adds clinical value net of nurse time, and a three-ward stagger with monthly audits is too small to support the 80% coverage decision rule.

codex.worst_flaw: The kiosk-linked reward is unfit for launch because aggregate counts can meet the 80% coverage threshold even when duplicate or unrelated entries substitute for unlogged observed hand cleaning.

holistic.reason: Unusually well-guarded design (audit-based reward, safeguards against over-logging, staggered randomised rollout, honest pilot framing), but the reward rule is long and conditional for nurses to grasp, a 30-minute break is a modest incentive, and the logging habit rests on fast-screen and feedback fixes with an uncertain coverage measure.

codex.worst_flaw: Teams with too few QA samples or CSAT responses have no defined fallback safety check, so rewards can continue while customer harm goes undetected.

claude.worst_flaw: The design leaves the existing CSAT bonus unchanged, so agents still have a reason to rush closures or send customers to an article, and it relies on a pause trigger after the fact instead of fixing that conflict. It also stacks a team threshold reward on public team progress and a director's recognition, with no plain-feedback arm to isolate what the reward adds, and no replayable event history or independent shadow validation of the count.

holistic.reason: Well-designed with workflow fixes, quality audits, CSAT guardrails and a staggered measurement plan, but a once-per-four-weeks team break is a weak, delayed motivator that agents may not notice, and 60-person team-level pooling invites free-riding while the setup is complex to run.

codex.worst_flaw: The same 45% payout threshold applies across queues even when their share of tickets with a useful knowledge-base opportunity differs, creating pressure to link marginal articles.

claude.worst_flaw: The team hour-off target of 45% is not tied to a diagnosed baseline or to feasibility by queue. The design also never checks the CSAT bonus as a competing incentive, even though it can push agents to close tickets fast instead of documenting them.

holistic.reason: Strong on measurement, QA, workflow fixes and CSAT protection, but a 45% team-wide target for one paid hour is a weak, diffuse incentive that many agents may not feel, the complex counting and staggered design add overhead, and the 40% keep-threshold after rewards end is ambitious given a 12% baseline.

codex.worst_flaw: Customer-data exposure is a launch blocker because the design specifies a reward pause after confirmed exposure and leaves prepublication privacy checks and immediate removal of exposed content undefined.

claude.worst_flaw: The team reward hinges on a flat 50% coverage target with no evidence it is feasible or valuable for each queue, and nothing says the 50% figure itself will be re-checked against baseline before it is announced. The CSAT bonus stays in pay, and the design never checks whether pressure to add articles could pull agents away from CSAT or how the two incentives interact, beyond a lagging CSAT-drop pause.

holistic.reason: Well-designed with quality sampling, CSAT guardrails, a pilot phase, and a control group, but a one-paid-hour team reward is modest, requires 50% coverage that may be hard in queues with few reusable cases, and the article-search fixes rather than the prize are what will drive lasting change.
